title: The Rhythm of the Seasons
author: Rebecca Foster
summary: Rebecca Foster's teaching transcript (edited by her husband Michael) explores the mega seasons of life -- youth and age, singleness and marriage, full nest and empty nest, scarcity and abundance -- through the lens of Ecclesiastes. Drawing on personal stories, she argues that human nature consistently longs for what it doesn't have while taking for granted what it prayed for, and that faithfulness requires receiving the present season rather than fantasizing about another. Youthful beauty fades, but a woman who walks with God develops spiritual beauty -- poise, grace, and the kind of presence that steadies a room -- that can take decades to mature. Singleness is not meaningless but an opportunity for undivided devotion. Marriage sanctifies, but Christ alone makes us whole. The transition from full nest to empty nest moves parents from commanders to coaches to consultants, and the empty season carries its own calling: to pour into younger women and the church rather than retreating to shallow pursuits. Scarcity teaches dependence; abundance tests gratitude. In both, Paul's lesson applies: 'I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content.'
points: * Ecclesiastes teaches the discipline of receiving the present season rather than fantasizing about the next: God appoints every season and wastes none of them. * Beauty fades, but spiritual beauty -- poise, grace, warmth, wisdom -- matures over decades; the most radiant women Foster has known have been grandmothers and elderly widows who still grew spiritually. * Singleness is real life: it brings freedom, focused spiritual growth, service, and an undivided ability to devote oneself to God -- and many women who are not single now may one day be single again. * The transition from full nest to empty nest shifts parents from commanders (young children) to coaches (older children) to consultants (grown children) -- and that last shift is often the hardest. * Scarcity teaches dependence on God; abundance tests gratitude and tempts toward self-sufficiency -- both seasons are necessary, and faithfulness requires walking well in both.
quotes: I remember when I prayed for what I now have.
Each new season reshapes what faithfulness requires.
Ecclesiastes teaches us to receive the season we are in instead of constantly fantasizing about another one. God appoints every season and wastes none of them.
Singleness is real life. It brings freedom, flexibility, focused spiritual growth, service, ministry, and a unique ability to devote yourself to the Lord.
Marriage is glorious, but it does not complete you or fix you. Christ alone makes you whole.
Parents move from commanders with small children to coaches with older children to consultants with grown children, and that last shift is often the hardest.

Faithfulness is the goal: to become the kind of woman who, whether she is fifteen or ninety-five, married or widowed, surrounded by children or sitting quietly in an empty house, can still say: 'The Lord has been good to me.'
